what_it_does: Quantum computers make errors constantly, so they rely on quantum error correction — a process of measuring groups of physical qubits and then running a classical decoder program to figure out what went wrong and fix it. To keep up with the quantum hardware in real time, decoders chop the stream of error measurements into overlapping time windows and process each window in parallel. The catch is that some windows cannot start until they know the outcome of the previous window, creating a chain of waiting that stretches out the total program time. SWIPER borrows an idea from classical computer design — branch prediction (guessing the outcome before you know it for certain) — and applies it here: the decoder guesses the dependency between adjacent windows and starts decoding speculatively, then corrects course if the guess was wrong, similar to how a CPU continues executing code after a branch before knowing which way the branch will go.
